name: Oak bark
habitat: Woodland, hedgerow and parkland across the temperate northern hemisphere.
identify: Lobed leaves — rounded lobes in the white-oak group, bristle-tipped points in the red-oak group.
Acorns sitting in a scaly cup. The cup is the family mark and no other tree here has one.
Deeply furrowed grey to brown bark on mature trunks.

lookalikes.name: Horse chestnut / buckeye
lookalikes.danger: Poisonous nuts; mistaking them for acorns is the classic error.
lookalikes.tell: Buckeye and horse chestnut nuts come out of a thick spiny or leathery husk and have NO scaly cup; their leaves are palmate, radiating from one point like fingers, not lobed.

preparations.method: Simmer a handful of chopped inner bark or young twig bark in water for 15-20 minutes until it is tea-dark.
preparations.for_use: An astringent wound wash, a gargle for sore throat, and a soak for weeping skin. Tannins bind protein and tighten tissue, which is what slows an ooze.

preparations.method: Apply the cooled boiled bark directly.
preparations.for_use: Weeping grazes, haemorrhoids, and stopping capillary ooze.

preparations.method: The same tannin solution, used long and cold.

cautions: Tannins are irritant in quantity — a strong decoction taken internally causes stomach upset and, sustained, kidney damage. Use it as a wash and a gargle, not as a daily drink.
Do not use a strong tannin wash inside a deep open wound; it damages the tissue trying to granulate.
Acorns must be leached before eating — see `food-acorn-leaching`.
evidence: Oak bark is an official astringent in several European pharmacopoeias for topical and gargle use. The tannin chemistry is well characterised.
